fields.title: A generated file keeps no record of the run that wrote it

sections.What we are doing instead: `kac generate --check` regenerates every block and index and compares the result against what is committed. [ctl-0007](https://github.com/paul80nd/knowledge-as-code/blob/a23ee6a1d78ea9df04c380fae75cb5d91b8530c6/examples/dog-fooding/controls/0007-corpus-validation.md) runs it on each pull request, and the workflow log records the run and its result. That log lives in GitHub Actions and expires there, and nothing keeps the result for longer.
sections.Why we need it: Nothing here has needed a run's result after its log expired. Keeping each result with the release it produced needs a step in the publish workflows and somewhere to put the output, and neither exists.
sections.What the risk is: A reader doubts a generated block or a published export after the run's log has expired, and nothing shows the run that produced it. Answering the doubt means checking out the commit and running the generator again.
sections.What compensates:
* `generate --check` fails the branch where any generated file is stale, so a stale file cannot land on `main`.
* The golden fixtures run `generate` over a corpus and compare the result, so the check has a test behind it.
* The generated block markers state the generator, so a reader can tell which command wrote the text.
* Every input is a committed file in the same repository, so the run's inputs are recoverable from the commit it ran
  on.
sections.How it closes: A run that publishes keeps its inputs, its output and its check result with the release it produced, and a standard states that it has to. This record closes on that standard.
sections.Scope: Every block between `BEGIN GENERATED` and `END GENERATED`, every `_index.md`, and the export `kac export` writes.
